A chord progression is a sequence of chords arranged to support melody and create harmonic motion in tonal music. It is the backbone of Western musical structure, organizing the movement from tension to resolution and providing the harmonic framework within which melody unfolds. Understanding chord progressions is essential to both composing and analyzing music from the Baroque era through pop and jazz.

A chord is a combination of three or more pitches sounded simultaneously. The most basic chords are the triads—three notes combining a root, third, and fifth—built on each degree of a scale. Chord progressions are named by Roman numerals indicating their scale-degree position: I for tonic, ii, iii, IV for subdominant, V for dominant, vi, and vii-diminished. Uppercase numerals indicate major chords, lowercase indicates minor chords.

The I-IV-V-I progression is the most fundamental in Western music. It moves from home at I to subdominant tension at IV, then to dominant tension at V, and back home. This cycle underlies countless classical, pop, and folk melodies. The I-vi-IV-V progression, or vi-IV-I-V, is ubiquitous in popular music and doo-wop; examples include "All You Need Is Love" and countless pop songs.

The twelve-bar blues progression, typically I-I-I-I-IV-IV-I-I-V-IV-I-V with variations, is the harmonic template for blues and jazz. It allows infinite melodic and improvisational variation over a fixed harmonic foundation. Understanding harmonic function—the role each chord plays, whether as tonic for rest, subdominant for departure, or dominant for tension toward resolution—makes progressions coherent and expressive.

The circle of fifths is a visual map of harmonic relationships. Chords a fifth apart are closely related, and progressions that follow the circle create natural forward motion. Through these structures and relationships, chord progressions provide the foundation for most Western music from the Baroque period to contemporary popular music.
